Signy
see-NYEE
n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Ardennes, founded in the 1130s, where William of Saint-Thierry was abbot and died)
From the locality in the Ardennes, Signy-l'Abbaye; a French place name, the village taking the abbey's name after it.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Signy in the Ardennes was founded in the 1130s in the Clairvaux filiation, and William of Saint-Thierry — who had resigned a Benedictine abbacy to become a Cistercian at Igny — became its abbot and died there about 1148. His best work was written at Signy, including the Epistola ad fratres de Monte Dei, the golden letter to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu, and a treatise on the nature and dignity of love. A man who gave up office, took it again in a poorer house, and spent his last years writing on the love of God has a claim on Protestant attention whatever one makes of his monasticism. The text for such a life is Paul's own summing up: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). Nothing of the abbey's church remains; the village of Signy-l'Abbaye keeps its name, which is the usual arrangement in France — the stones go and the toponym stays.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines course as a passing, a moving, the progress of any thing, also the ground run or passed over; finish as to arrive at the end of, to bring to an end; and faith as the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another.

expand to see more

COURSE, n. A passing; a moving, or motion forward; the ground, way or path run or passed over; also, the progress of any thing; manner of proceeding.

FINISH, v.t. To arrive at the end of, in a literal sense; to complete; to bring to an end; to perfect.

FAITH, n. The assent of the mind or understanding to the truth of what God has revealed; also, evangelical, justifying, or saving faith.

FIGHT, n. A battle; an engagement; a contest in arms; also, a struggle or contention of any kind.

ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

2Ti 4:8 — "Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing."

Act 20:24 — "But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God."

1Co 9:24 — "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain."

Modern Corruption

An Ardennes abbey where William of Saint-Thierry was abbot and died: a man who laid down office, took it again in a poorer house, and wrote on the love of God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the finishing of a course. “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing” (2Ti 4:8) extends Paul's confidence to every believer and withholds it from nobody who loves Christ's return.

The live corruption is unfinished Christianity: enthusiasm at the start, a long middle, and no account taken of the end. Paul kept the end in view and ran accordingly — “so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus” (Act 20:24), and “So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dromos (G1408), a course or race; Greek agon (G73), a contest; Greek teleo (G5055), to finish; Greek stephanos (G4735), a crown; Greek pistis (G4102), faith.

expand to see more

Greek dromos (G1408) — a running course; “I have finished my course” (2Ti 4:7).

Greek agon (G73) — a contest, a fight; the noun behind Paul's good fight.

Greek teleo (G5055) — to finish, complete; the verb of a life brought to its end.

Greek stephanos (G4735) — a victor's wreath; “a crown of righteousness” (2Ti 4:8).

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; “I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7).

Usage

"“I have fought a good fight” (2Ti 4:7) — the text for a finished life."

"“that I might finish my course with joy” (Act 20:24) — the end kept in view throughout."

"“So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24) — the manner of running that reaches it."
